Teacher recording notes: Welcome to today's lesson: Lesson 7.1: Anne of Green Gables (Ch. 1). In your warm-up, you'll focus on 📚 What Good Readers Do — Distinguish narrator point of view from character perspective. As you read, pay close attention to the characters' actions and motivations. Think about how events connect to the bigger ideas in the story. Use your journal to capture your thoughts and any questions that come up.
1
📚 What Good Readers Do
Distinguish narrator point of view from character perspective

Every story has a narrator — the voice telling you what happens — and inside the story, characters who each see things their own way. Keeping those two apart lets you notice when a character is certain about something the narrator quietly shows is wrong.

💡

How to Do It:

  1. Find the voice: Ask who is telling this. Is it someone inside the story, or a voice outside it that can see everyone?
  2. Separate the opinion: When you read a judgment about someone, decide whether the narrator said it or a character thinks it.
  3. Check it against the facts: Ask what the narrator lets you see that the character does not know yet.
🧠 As you read today, watch for:

As you read Ch. 1, keep an eye on Mrs. Rachel Lynde. She is curious about Matthew and sure she knows what he must be up to. Which parts of the chapter are her opinions, and which parts does the narrator tell you straight? What does the narrator let you notice about her that she would never say about herself?

💭 Think about this as you read today — you don't need to write anything here.

🔧 Now fix this one
mrs rachel lynde walked through avonlea every morning
Use the model above to help you. Rewrite this sentence correctly in your notebook.

Corrected: Mrs. Rachel Lynde walked through Avonlea every morning.

Same structure: capital letters on the title + names (Mrs. Rachel Lynde), capital letter on the place name (Avonlea), and a period at the end. Common nouns like "morning" stay lowercase.

🔤 Vocabulary
Words from this week's chapters.

When you meet a word you don't know, use these three steps in order:

📌 Let's try it together: "companion"
1
Read the Sentence
Find the word in the book. What clues does the sentence give you?
"With this, Matthew's companion stopped talking for a moment."
Matthew is in the buggy with Anne. The author calls Anne his companion — the person riding along with him. So companion must describe someone who goes with you, who keeps you company.
2
Look at the Word Parts
Do you see a root, prefix, or suffix you recognize?
com- + pan + -ion
Three parts: com- (together) + pan (from a Latin word meaning bread) + -ion (one who). Long ago, a companion was someone you shared bread with. So companion = someone who shares life with you.
3
Confirm
Were we close?
✅ Companion means someone you spend time with — a friend or partner. Our context and word parts got us there!

Plurals from Chapters 1 and 2. Two very different habits.

💭

Think it through.

  1. Which ones follow the ordinary -s rule?
  2. Which ones change in a way you simply have to remember?
  3. What would you call each group?
🎯

Directions: Drag each one into the column where you think it belongs, then name the two groups yourself.

child → childrenroad → roadswoman → womengable → gablesfoot → feetwindow → windows
Group A
Group B

Group A are regular — add -s and you are done.

Group B are irregular. Child/children, woman/women, foot/feet change inside the word. No rule will generate them; they have to be known.

🪶 Show What You Know

4
🔠 Spelling: Plural Endings (-s, -es, y→ies)
Discover the pattern by listening.
Group A — just add -s

cat → cats · road → roads · book → books · tree → trees

Group B — add -es OR change y to i + es

box → boxes · brush → brushes · puppy → puppies · story → stories

👂 Say them out loud

Group A words: how do you make them plural? What changes?

Group B: box and brush get -es. Why not just -s? (Try saying "boxs" — it doesn't work.)

Group B: puppy becomes puppies. What changes about the ending? Look at the last letter of the singular.

Look at these two groups of words:

Most nouns just add -s for plural (cats, roads, books).

Nouns ending in -s, -x, -sh, -ch, -z add -es (boxes, brushes, churches) — because -s alone would be hard to say.

Nouns ending in a consonant + y change the y to i and add -es (puppy → puppies, story → stories).

🎮

Practice: Sort these words using the pattern you discovered.

cats boxes roads stories trees brushes
Just add -s
-es or y→ies

Growing-Up Watch: IMAGINATION & WONDER
One aspect of growing up Anne shows us this week
💎 What is imagination & wonder?

Imagination is the gift of making the world bigger with your words and your eyes.

🪶 Anne's moment:

Anne arrives at Green Gables with nothing — no parents, no home of her own, and the news she might be sent back. But on the drive from the train station, she renames a plain road "The White Way of Delight" and a small pond "The Lake of Shining Waters." Her life is hard. Her imagination makes it bearable. It even makes it beautiful.

💭 Think: How does YOUR character use imagination, or wonder, or naming things to survive hard moments?

Writer’s Workshop: Week 7 · VOICE
Brainstorm + Character Voice
★ Voice ○ Character ○ Conflict ○ Draft Open ○ Rising Action ○ Revise ○ Edit ○ Publish
🎯

Today’s focus: Today: VOICE. Every great character sounds like a real person, not a list of facts. Pick SPECIFIC WORDS — vivid verbs and descriptive adjectives — that match your character’s personality.

👀 Watch How — Meet Sam, our example writer

Meet Sam. Sam is a 4th-grade writer just starting a realistic-fiction story about Mateo Hernandez, a kid who’s scared to try out for the soccer team. Today, Sam works on Mateo’s VOICE — choosing specific words.

BEFORE
Mateo was nervous. He looked at the field. He felt bad.
AFTER
Mateo’s hands felt cold. He stared at the field, kicking dirt with his toe. “Don’t throw up,” he whispered to himself.

Notice: Sam’s second version uses SPECIFIC, VIVID words: hands felt cold, stared, kicking dirt, don’t throw up. Specific words show us Mateo’s feelings instead of just telling us.

📋 Today’s Tool: Specific Words

Great writing has words that are specific, vivid, and descriptive.

🪶 Sentence Frames You Can Borrow

Stuck on how to start? Try one of these:

  • “[Character]’s [body part] felt ___.”
  • “[Character] [vivid verb]-ed ___.”
  • “‘___,’ [character] whispered/shouted/mumbled.”
  • “The ___ was [specific adjective].”
